summary: Defines a Uniform Resource Name namespace for UUIDs (also called GUIDs), 128-bit identifiers that can be generated without central coordination and are meant to be unique across space and time. The format comes from the Apollo and DCE systems and was later used on Microsoft Windows. It was replaced by RFC 9562.

plainLanguage.summary: A UUID is a 128-bit number used as a unique label for something. Because it can be generated on demand without asking anyone, two systems that have never spoken to each other can still create labels that will not collide. This RFC fixes the bit layout, the three generation methods, and the text form urn:uuid:.

questions: how is a version 1 uuid generated
subtitle: A 128-bit identifier format that guarantees uniqueness without any central registration, and its URN form.

tldr.problem: Systems that hand out identifiers to unrelated objects need the identifiers to be unique without asking a central authority first, and to stay unique over time.
tldr.mechanism: A UUID is 128 bits divided into a timestamp, a clock sequence, a node identifier and a version marker, with the bits laid out so that a reader can tell which of several generation methods produced it. The RFC defines three methods: from the time and the machine's hardware address, from a hash of a name, and from random numbers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4122 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 9562.

today: RFC 4122 was a Proposed Standard published in July 2005. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 9562.

sections.title: What a UUID Is
sections.content:
This specification defines a Uniform Resource Name namespace for UUIDs, also known as GUIDs. A UUID is 128 bits long, requires no central registration process, and can guarantee uniqueness across space and time. UUIDs were originally used in the Apollo Network Computing System, later in the Open Software Foundation's Distributed Computing Environment, and then in Microsoft Windows platforms.

The main reason for using UUIDs is that no centralized authority is required to administer them, although one format uses IEEE 802 node identifiers and others do not. As a result, generation on demand can be completely automated. The generation algorithm described in the RFC supports allocation rates of up to 10 million per second per machine if necessary, so that UUIDs could even be used as transaction identifiers.

UUIDs are of a fixed size, 128 bits, which is reasonably small compared with other alternatives. That lends itself well to sorting, ordering and hashing of all kinds, to storing in databases, to simple allocation, and to ease of programming in general. Since UUIDs are unique and persistent, they make excellent Uniform Resource Names: the ability to generate a new UUID without a registration process makes them one of the URNs with the lowest minting cost.

The document is written as a concise guide for those wishing to implement services using UUIDs as URNs. Nothing in it overrides the DCE standards that defined UUIDs, and there is an ITU-T Recommendation and ISO/IEC standard derived from earlier versions of the document, with the two sets of specifications aligned and fully technically compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: A UUID is a 128-bit label for something. Because a program can make one up on its own, without asking anyone, two unrelated systems can both hand out labels that will not clash. The fixed size also makes them easy to store, sort and hash.

sections.title: The Bit Layout of a UUID
sections.content:
The UUID format is 16 octets, and some bits of the eight octet variant field determine the finer structure. The fields are presented with the most significant one first: time_low is an unsigned 32-bit integer in octets 0 to 3, the low field of the timestamp; time_mid is an unsigned 16-bit integer in octets 4 and 5, the middle field of the timestamp; time_hi_and_version is an unsigned 16-bit integer in octets 6 and 7, the high field of the timestamp multiplexed with the version number; clock_seq_hi_and_reserved is an unsigned 8-bit integer in octet 8, the high field of the clock sequence multiplexed with the variant; clock_seq_low is an unsigned 8-bit integer in octet 9; and node is an unsigned 48-bit integer in octets 10 to 15, the spatially unique node identifier. Each field is encoded with the most significant byte first, in network byte order.

The variant field consists of a variable number of the most significant bits of octet 8 and determines the layout of the whole UUID: the interpretation of all other bits depends on it. The variant defined in this document has the bits 1, 0 and don't-care; the other three patterns are reserved for NCS backward compatibility, Microsoft Corporation backward compatibility, and future definition. Interoperability with the other variants is not guaranteed.

The version number is in the most significant 4 bits of the timestamp. Version 1 is the time-based version defined in this document, version 2 is the DCE Security version with embedded POSIX UIDs, version 3 is the name-based version that uses MD5 hashing, version 4 is the randomly or pseudo-randomly generated version, and version 5 is the name-based version that uses SHA-1 hashing.

The timestamp is a 60-bit value. For version 1 it is Coordinated Universal Time counted in 100-nanosecond intervals since 00:00:00.00, 15 October 1582, the date of the Gregorian reform. For versions 3 and 5 it is constructed from a name, and for version 4 it is randomly generated. The clock sequence helps avoid duplicates when the clock is set backwards or the node ID changes: it is a 14-bit value that must be initialized once in the lifetime of a system to a random number, not correlated with the node identifier, and incremented when the clock has been set backwards. The node field holds an IEEE 802 MAC address for version 1, with the multicast bit set when a random value is used instead. The nil UUID is the special form with all 128 bits set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The 128 bits are split into fixed pieces: a timestamp, a clock sequence, a machine identifier, and two small fields that record which version and which layout are in use. The version field is what lets a program tell how the identifier was made.

sections.title: Three Ways to Generate a UUID
sections.content:
The first algorithm creates a time-based, version 1 UUID. The basic version is simple, correct and inefficient: take a system-wide lock, read the generator state, which holds the timestamp, clock sequence and node ID used for the last UUID, from a stable store such as a file; get the current time as a 60-bit count of 100-nanosecond intervals since 15 October 1582 and the current node ID; if the state was unavailable or the saved node ID differs from the current one, generate a random clock sequence value; if the state was available but the saved timestamp is later than the current one, increment the clock sequence; save the state back and release the lock. The UUID is then formatted from the timestamp, clock sequence and node ID. The RFC points out that reading and writing the state each time is inefficient, that the system clock may not have 100-nanosecond resolution, and that sharing state across process boundaries may be inefficient, and offers a modular fix for each: read the state once at boot time, simulate a high resolution timestamp by counting how many UUIDs share the same system time, write the stable store less often, and allocate blocks of timestamps to processes that share the generator.

The second algorithm creates a name-based, version 3 or version 5 UUID from names that are drawn from, and unique within, some namespace. Examples of namespaces are the domain name system, URLs, ISO Object IDs, X.500 Distinguished Names, and reserved words in a programming language. The requirements are that UUIDs generated at different times from the same name in the same namespace must be equal, that UUIDs from two different names in the same namespace should be different with very high probability, that UUIDs from the same name in two different namespaces should be different with very high probability, and that two equal name-based UUIDs must have come from the same name in the same namespace with very high probability. The algorithm allocates a UUID to use as the namespace ID, chooses MD5 or SHA-1 as the hash algorithm, with SHA-1 preferred if backward compatibility is not an issue, converts the name to a canonical sequence of octets, puts the namespace ID in network byte order, computes the hash of the namespace ID concatenated with the name, and then copies the hash octets into the fields of the UUID and sets the version number.

The third algorithm creates a version 4 UUID from truly random or pseudo-random numbers: set the two most significant bits of clock_seq_hi_and_reserved to zero and one, set the four most significant bits of time_hi_and_version to the version number 4, and set all the other bits to randomly or pseudo-randomly chosen values.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to make one. Version 1 uses the clock and the machine's own hardware address, keeping a note of the last value so it never repeats. Version 3 and 5 hash a name together with a namespace, so the same name always gives the same identifier. Version 4 is just random bits.

sections.title: Writing a UUID as a URN
sections.content:
A UUID is an identifier that is unique across both space and time with respect to the space of all UUIDs. Because a UUID is a fixed size and contains a time field, it is possible for values to roll over, around A.D. 3400 depending on the algorithm used. A UUID can be used for many purposes, from tagging objects with an extremely short lifetime to reliably identifying very persistent objects across a network.

The internal representation of a UUID is a specific sequence of bits in memory. To represent a UUID as a URN it is necessary to convert that bit sequence into a string. Each field is treated as an integer and its value is printed as a zero-filled hexadecimal digit string with the most significant digit first, with the hexadecimal values a to f written in lower case and read case-insensitively.

The formal definition of the string representation is given in ABNF: a UUID is time-low, a hyphen, time-mid, a hyphen, time-high-and-version, a hyphen, clock-seq-and-reserved, clock-seq-low, a hyphen and node, where time-low is 4 hex octets, time-mid and time-high-and-version are 2 hex octets each, clock-seq-and-reserved and clock-seq-low are one hex octet each, and node is 6 hex octets. The example given of the string representation of a UUID as a URN is urn:uuid:f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6.

Two UUIDs are equal if and only if all their corresponding fields are equal, comparing each field as an unsigned integer in order of significance. As an implementation note, equality comparison can be performed on many systems by doing the appropriate byte-order canonicalization and then treating the two UUIDs as 128-bit unsigned integers. UUIDs can also be ordered lexicographically: for a pair, the first follows the second if the most significant field in which they differ is greater for the first.
sections.plainLanguage: The text form is a fixed pattern of hexadecimal digits and hyphens, wrapped in urn:uuid:. Two UUIDs are the same when all their fields match, and they can be put in order by comparing the fields from the most significant one down.

sections.title: What a UUID Is Not
sections.content:
The RFC is direct about the limits of a UUID. Do not assume that UUIDs are hard to guess; they should not be used as security capabilities, meaning identifiers whose mere possession grants access. A predictable random number source will make the situation worse.

Do not assume that it is easy to determine if a UUID has been slightly transposed in order to redirect a reference to another object. Humans do not have the ability to easily check the integrity of a UUID by simply glancing at it.

Distributed applications generating UUIDs at a variety of hosts must be willing to rely on the random number source at all hosts. If this is not feasible, the namespace variant should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: A UUID is an identifier, not a secret. It is not hard to guess, so it must not be used as a password or a token, and a mistyped UUID is not something a reader will notice by eye.

fields.name: time_low
fields.desc: Unsigned 32-bit integer: the low field of the timestamp.

fields.name: time_mid
fields.desc: Unsigned 16-bit integer: the middle field of the timestamp.

fields.name: time_hi_and_version
fields.desc: The high field of the timestamp, with the version number in its top four bits.

fields.name: clock_seq_hi_and_reserved
fields.desc: The high field of the clock sequence, with the variant in its top bits.

fields.name: clock_seq_low
fields.desc: The low field of the clock sequence.

fields.name: node
fields.desc: The spatially unique node identifier, usually an IEEE 802 MAC address.

items.label: Time-based
items.desc: Built from a timestamp, a clock sequence and a node identifier.

items.label: DCE Security
items.desc: The DCE Security version, with embedded POSIX UIDs.

items.label: Name-based, MD5
items.desc: A hash of a name in a namespace, using MD5.

items.label: Random
items.desc: Truly random or pseudo-randomly chosen bits.

items.label: Name-based, SHA-1
items.desc: A hash of a name in a namespace, using SHA-1.

viz.caption: THE STRING FORM OF A UUID (SECTION 3)

data.title: ABNF of the UUID string representation
data.code:
UUID                   = time-low "-" time-mid "-"
                         time-high-and-version "-"
                         clock-seq-and-reserved
                         clock-seq-low "-" node
time-low               = 4hexOctet
time-mid               = 2hexOctet
time-high-and-version  = 2hexOctet
clock-seq-and-reserved = hexOctet
clock-seq-low          = hexOctet
node                   = 6hexOctet
